reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Von Noorden's Binocular Vision and Ocular Motility
clinicalPearls: Onset is within the first months of life, and the nystagmus is typically conjugate, horizontal, and remains horizontal even on up- or down-gaze (uniplanar)
A null zone exists where the oscillation dampens and vision is best, prompting a compensatory anomalous head posture
The nystagmus characteristically dampens with convergence and increases with fixation effort or anxiety
Oscillopsia is usually absent, in contrast to acquired nystagmus
Eye-movement recordings show characteristic waveforms with an accelerating (increasing-velocity) slow phase
It may be idiopathic (motor) or sensory, the latter associated with albinism, achromatopsia, Leber congenital amaurosis, optic nerve hypoplasia, or aniridia
A careful search for an afferent visual defect is essential, as sensory causes carry different prognoses

Management includes correcting refractive error and amblyopia, prisms to shift the null zone toward primary position, and null-zone-repositioning surgery (Kestenbaum-Anderson) for a significant head posture
reference.pathophysiology: Infantile nystagmus reflects instability of the ocular motor fixation-maintenance system, producing involuntary rhythmic to-and-fro eye movements from early life. In sensory forms an afferent visual deficit such as albinism, a retinal dystrophy, or optic nerve hypoplasia degrades the fixation signal that normally stabilises gaze; in idiopathic (motor) forms the afferent pathway is intact and the defect lies in ocular motor control itself. A null zone develops where slow-phase drift is minimised, and the brain adopts a head turn to keep the eyes in that position, optimising visual acuity.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired nystagmus, which is neurological and associated with oscillopsia
Spasmus nutans with nystagmus, head nodding, and torticollis
Nystagmus of oculocutaneous or ocular albinism
Sensory nystagmus from congenital cataract or other media opacity
Downbeat or gaze-evoked nystagmus of posterior fossa disease
additionalInvestigations: Detailed ocular and orthoptic examination including head-posture and null-zone assessment
Cycloplegic refraction and best-corrected visual acuity
Slit-lamp and dilated fundus examination for iris transillumination, foveal hypoplasia, and optic nerve anomalies
Electrodiagnostic testing (electroretinogram and visual evoked potentials) for suspected sensory causes
Eye-movement recording to characterise the waveform where available
Neuroimaging if features suggest an acquired or neurological cause
redFlags: Oscillopsia, vertical or dissociated nystagmus, or other neurological signs suggesting acquired disease
Asymmetric or unilateral nystagmus with head nodding requiring exclusion of intracranial pathology
Poor vision suggesting a significant underlying retinal or optic nerve disorder
Rapid change in the nystagmus pattern or new onset in an older child
reference.prognosis: Idiopathic infantile nystagmus is compatible with useful, often good, vision that tends to stabilise with age; visual outcome in sensory forms is determined by the underlying afferent disorder, and head-posture surgery can meaningfully improve an abnormal head position.
pitfalls: Assuming all infantile nystagmus is benign and missing an underlying sensory or neurological cause
Failing to correct refractive error and treat amblyopia
Overlooking a subtle anomalous head posture that indicates a shiftable null zone
Misinterpreting a compensatory head turn as a primary musculoskeletal (torticollis) problem
references: Von Noorden's Binocular Vision and Ocular Motility
management: Full cycloplegic spectacle correction of refractive error to optimise the degraded fixation signal
Manage amblyopia and treat any underlying sensory cause such as albinism or a retinal dystrophy identified on electrodiagnostics
Kestenbaum-Anderson eye-muscle surgery to shift the null zone and correct a compensatory anomalous head posture
Prisms to move the image toward the null zone or promote convergence damping
Low-vision aids and support where acuity is limited by a sensory cause
Ophthalmology and orthoptic follow-up through visual development
Genetic counselling where an inherited sensory or idiopathic cause is confirmed
